claims.text: A controlled gradient of trace Nb or Mo at CrMnFeCoNi multilayer interfaces enhances chemical short-range ordering.
Interfacial Nb or Mo doping strengthens bonding between the layers.
Enhanced interfacial ordering and bonding elevate the energy barrier for dislocation transmission across interfaces.
The proposed interfacial modification lowers the steady-state creep rate under sustained thermal and mechanical loading.
The proposed interfacial modification delays the onset of plastic deformation under sustained thermal and mechanical loading.
The baseline coatings have well-defined undoped interfaces with standard interfacial bonding and chemical ordering.
The refractory dopant can be localized at interface regions while minimally disturbing overall phase stability.
Dopant segregation at layer boundaries increases interfacial cohesion.
Increasing interfacial cohesive strength raises the barrier to dislocation motion across interfaces.
The raised barrier to interfacial dislocation motion suppresses localized shear-band activation.
Localized shear-band activation typically leads to time-dependent plastic deformation in these coatings.
Doped coatings should exhibit a lower steady-state creep rate than undoped coatings.
Doped coatings should exhibit a later onset of plastic deformation than undoped coatings.
The proposed mechanism applies only when doping does not cause unwanted phase transformations or substantial non-interfacial microstructural changes.
The proposed mechanism is primarily applicable under sustained loading at moderate to high temperatures.
A lack of statistically significant creep-rate reduction and deformation delay in the doped coating would falsify the proposed performance effect.
A lack of correlation between interfacial chemical ordering and improved creep performance would falsify the claim that ordering governs resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
